lines.text: You had memories as a baby. You just can't reach them.
Ask anyone for their first memory, and it usually starts around age three.
Before that? Almost blank. Scientists call it infantile amnesia.
For decades, the explanation was simple: a baby brain was too young to record anything.
Then in twenty twenty-five, Yale scientists scanned twenty-six babies' brains while they looked at pictures.
The harder the memory center fired the first time, the more the baby recognized that picture later.
That worked best after about age one.
Baby mice point the same way: memories that seemed lost came back when scientists switched on the right brain cells.
So the memories may be saved. The hard part may be finding them.
Scientists still don't know how long baby memories last.
